title: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order of all elements in O(log(min(m, n))) time, without actually merging the arrays.
shortTitle: Median of Two Sorted Arrays — Binary Search Partition

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time uses a binary search that partitions both arrays so that the left combined half and the right combined half are correctly balanced in count and value. We binary-search the cut position in the smaller array, deriving the cut in the larger array, until every element on the left is less than or equal to every element on the right. This achieves O(log(min(m, n))) time.
s1_definition.analogy: Two sorted ledgers must be combined to find the middle value, but merging them fully would be slow. Instead the clerk draws a vertical cut line through both ledgers at once such that the total number of rows left of the cut equals the number right of it, and every value on the left is no larger than every value on the right. The median is then read directly from the values adjacent to the cut.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search a partition of the smaller array so the two combined halves are balanced; read the median at the boundary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time uses a binary search that partitions both arrays so that the left combined half and the right combined half are correctly balanced in count and value. We binary-search the cut position in the smaller array, deriving the cut in the larger array, until every element on the left is less than or equal to every element on the right. This achieves O(log(min(m, n))) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two sorted ledgers must be combined to find the middle value, but merging them fully would be slow. Instead the clerk draws a vertical cut line through both ledgers at once such that the total number of rows left of the cut equals the number right of it, and every value on the left is no larger than every value on the right. The median is then read directly from the values adjacent to the cut.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search a partition of the smaller array so the two combined halves are balanced; read the median at the boundary.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach merges both arrays in O(m plus n) and reads the middle, but the optimal approach never merges. It binary-searches a partition point in the smaller array and computes the complementary partition in the larger array so the left side always holds exactly half the total elements.

We always search the smaller array to keep the range tiny. Let the smaller array be A of length m and the larger be B of length n. We pick a cut i in A, then the cut in B is j equals (m plus n plus 1) over 2 minus i, which guarantees the left side has the correct count for both odd and even totals.

We define four boundary values around the cuts: the largest on A's left is A[i minus 1] or negative infinity if i is zero; the smallest on A's right is A[i] or positive infinity if i equals m; similarly for B with j. The partition is correct when A-left-max is less than or equal to B-right-min and B-left-max is less than or equal to A-right-min. This is the condition that everything left is no greater than everything right.

If A-left-max is greater than B-right-min, the cut i is too far right, so we move high to i minus 1; if B-left-max is greater than A-right-min, i is too far left, so we move low to i plus 1. We binary-search i over the range 0 to m.

Once balanced, for an odd total the median is the max of the two left-side values; for an even total it is the average of the max of the lefts and the min of the rights.

A senior-level nuance is handling the infinities at the array edges, which gracefully covers empty partitions without special branches. Another nuance is always searching the shorter array, which bounds the time at log of the smaller length and also keeps the derived cut j within bounds.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India keeps two sorted transaction-amount datasets, one from the savings system and one from the current-account system, and the analytics team needs the median transaction amount across both combined to report a typical transaction size. Fully merging two very large sorted datasets just to find the middle value is wasteful. This is exactly the median-of-two-sorted-arrays problem.

Problem 2 — The datasets are large and the median query is frequent, so we need the logarithmic partition method rather than an O(m plus n) merge.

Problem 3 — The combined count can be odd or even, so the median is either a single middle value or the average of the two central values, which the partition boundaries give directly.

In the code: a `MedianAnalyzer` holds a method taking two sorted int arrays. A `findMedian` method performs the partition binary search. A `MedianDemo` main computes the median for an odd combined length and an even combined length.

sections.s5_journey:
Input odd case: savings 1000, 3000, 5000 and current 2000, 4000. Combined sorted is 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, and the median is 3000.

Step 1: a is current (length 2, the smaller) and b is savings (length 3). m is 2, n is 3, halfLen is (2 plus 3 plus 1) over 2 which is 3.

Step 2: low 0, high 2, i equals 1, so j equals 3 minus 1 equals 2. aLeftMax is a[0] 2000, aRightMin is a[1] 4000, bLeftMax is b[1] 3000, bRightMin is b[2] 5000.

Step 3: Check: aLeftMax 2000 is at most bRightMin 5000, and bLeftMax 3000 is at most aRightMin 4000. Both hold, so the partition is correct.

Step 4: Total 5 is odd, so median is the max of the left values, max of 2000 and 3000, which is 3000.

For the even case the partition balances to give the average of the two central values 2000 and 3000, which is 2500.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 22:50:00 [INFO] Median across combined datasets (odd total count)
2026-10-26 22:50:00 [INFO] Median -> 3000.0
2026-10-26 22:50:00 [INFO] Median across combined datasets (even total count)
2026-10-26 22:50:00 [INFO] Median -> 2500.0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: a(smaller)=[2000 4000]  b=[1000 3000 5000]  (combined 5, odd)
  halfLen = (2+3+1)/2 = 3
    │
    ▼ binary search cut i in a; j = halfLen - i
  i=1 j=2:
    aLeft=2000 | aRight=4000
    bLeft=3000 | bRight=5000
    2000≤5000 and 3000≤4000  → balanced
    │
    ▼ odd → median = max(aLeft,bLeft) = max(2000,3000)
  Output: 3000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time is one of the hardest binary-search problems, and the key idea is that I never actually merge the arrays. Instead I binary-search a partition position. I draw a cut through both arrays at once such that the left side holds exactly half of all the elements combined, and I adjust the cut until every element on the left is less than or equal to every element on the right. Once that balance holds, the median sits right at the boundary: for an odd total it is the larger of the two left-edge values, and for an even total it is the average of the larger left-edge value and the smaller right-edge value.

The mechanics are that I always binary-search the smaller of the two arrays to keep the search range as short as possible, and I derive the cut in the larger array from the cut in the smaller one using the half-length formula, so the two halves always have the right counts for both odd and even totals. If the left side of the smaller array reaches too high compared to the right side of the larger array, my cut is too far right and I move it left, and vice versa.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, the analytics team needs the median transaction amount across two sorted datasets, one from the savings system and one from the current-account system, to report a typical transaction size. Fully merging two very large sorted datasets just to read the middle value would be wasteful, so this partition method gives the median in time logarithmic in the smaller dataset.

The detail that makes the code clean is using negative and positive infinity as sentinels at the array edges, which handles the cases where a partition is empty on one side without any special branching. And always searching the shorter array is not just an optimization; it also guarantees the derived cut in the longer array stays within bounds, which keeps the algorithm correct as well as fast.
